name: Mayuranathaswami Temple, Mayiladuthurai
deity: Shiva as Mayuranathar, with the goddess Abhayambikai
period: Great Shaiva temple on the Kaveri, sung in the Tevaram (7th century), with Chola and later work
summary: On the bank of the Kaveri at Mayiladuthurai, Shiva is Mayuranathar, named for Parvati's worship here in the form of a peahen (mayil); the town and temple take their name from her dance of penance.

sections.history: Mayiladuthurai, the town where the peahen danced, is a great Shaiva centre on the north bank of the Kaveri, and its Mayuranathaswami temple is a Paadal Petra Sthalam praised by Appar and Thirugnana Sambandar, counted among the shrines sung on the southern side of the river's course. Chola inscriptions call the deity Thirumayiladuthurai Udaiyar, and the temple was built and enriched in stone by the Cholas and their successors, with later addition by the Nayaks and others. In the fifteenth century the poet Arunagirinathar praised it in his Tirupugazh. The temple is administered by the Thiruvavaduthurai Adheenam and remains one of the foremost temples of the delta.
sections.architecture: The temple is a large Dravidian complex entered through a towering rajagopuram, with spacious prakara courtyards, pillared halls and a temple tank. The sanctum enshrines the Shiva linga of Mayuranathar, and the goddess Abhayambikai has her own shrine. Around the courtyards stand the shrines of the parivara deities and the saints, and the riverside ghats of the Kaveri lie close by, used for the great bathing festivals. The scale and the layered additions mark it as one of the major temples of the Kaveri country.
sections.legends: The temple's name comes from Parvati. In the legend she once slighted Shiva, or playfully covered his eyes, and was asked to do penance; taking the form of a peahen, mayil, she worshipped Shiva on the bank of the Kaveri here and danced before him, and the Lord in turn is said to have danced the Gowri Thandava for her. From her worship as the peahen the Lord became Mayuranathar and the town Mayiladuthurai, the place where the peahen danced, and Parvati won back her union with Shiva.
sections.festivals: The temple is renowned for Tula Snanam, the sacred bathing in the Kaveri in the Tamil month of Aippasi (Tula), when great crowds gather at the river ghats, a festival for which Mayiladuthurai is especially famous. Maha Shivaratri, the monthly Pradosham, and the car festival are also observed. Festival dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Mayuranathaswami is a busy, living temple at the heart of its town, and a visit often joins the temple to the Kaveri ghats a short walk away, where pilgrims bathe, especially in the Tula month. Within the walls the great halls and the shrines of Mayuranathar and Abhayambikai reward an unhurried round, and the story of the peahen's dance gives the place its gentle name and spirit.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Mayiladuthurai is a major town on the Kaveri in Mayiladuthurai district, with its own railway junction on the Chennai–Thanjavur line. Tiruchirappalli airport is about 110 km away. The temple is in the heart of town, within walking distance of the bus stand and railway station.
